title: Google Search
brief: Design a web search engine like Google Search: type a few words and get the best pages in a fraction of a second, from an index far too big for one machine. This is a design from general, public ideas about search engines. Real internals are not public, and this page does not claim to describe them.

functional: Take a text query and return a ranked page of results with titles and snippets.
Find documents that contain all the query words, over a huge web index.
Correct spelling and understand simple synonyms.
Show new content such as breaking news within minutes.
Keep the index up to date as pages are crawled again.

evolution.title: One machine, an inverted index
evolution.problem: Scanning every page for the query words would take hours. Start with the simplest thing that works: one box.
evolution.change: Offline, the crawler feeds an indexer that tokenises each page and builds an inverted index: for each word, a sorted posting list of the documents that contain it. A query reads the lists for its words and intersects them.

evolution.title: Shard by document
evolution.problem: Tens of billions of pages are far more than one machine can store, and one machine's CPU cannot serve the query rate.
evolution.change: Split documents across shards. Each shard holds a full index for its own documents, so every shard can answer every query. An aggregator sends the query to all shards at once (scatter) and merges the answers (gather).
evolution.numbers: shards = documents divided by documents per shard

evolution.title: Two-pass ranking
evolution.problem: Millions of documents match a common query. Scoring each with an expensive model blows the time budget.
evolution.change: Each shard scores cheaply and returns its best few hundred. The aggregator merges them. A re-ranker applies the slow, rich model to only the top candidates, then the document store fills in snippets.

evolution.title: Cache hot queries
evolution.problem: A small set of popular queries is asked again and again, and each costs a fan-out to every shard.
evolution.change: Cache the final results of normalised queries for a short time. Shards also keep hot posting lists in memory.
evolution.numbers: shard requests per second = queries times shards

evolution.title: Query understanding
evolution.problem: People mistype words and use different words for the same thing. Exact matching returns nothing, or misses good pages.
evolution.change: A query understanding block fixes spelling, adds synonyms and detects the language before the query reaches the index. It is one dictionary lookup and a few rules, not a new index.

evolution.title: A fresh tier
evolution.problem: Building the big index takes hours, but news pages must be searchable in minutes.
evolution.change: Keep a small fast-updating index for new and changing pages. The aggregator queries it alongside the big shards and merges, so recent items appear fast while the big index stays immutable and optimised.

steps.say: The browser sends the query to the frontend.
The frontend normalises the query and checks the result cache. A hit returns right here.
On a miss, query understanding fixes spelling and adds synonyms.
The aggregator receives the rewritten query and sets a deadline for the whole fan-out.
It sends the query to every shard at the same moment. Each shard intersects the posting lists of its own documents.
It also asks the small fresh index for recent matches.
Each shard returns its local top results with a cheap score. The aggregator merges them into one global list and does not wait for stragglers past the deadline.
The re-ranker scores only the top few hundred with the expensive model.
It fetches titles and snippets for the final ten.
The page goes back to the frontend, is cached, and is shown to the user.
The crawler downloads a page. How it decides what to fetch is the Web Crawler design.
The indexer parses the page, strips markup and splits it into tokens: lowercased, stemmed words.
For each token it records the document id and positions. Together these entries form posting lists.
A page that is new or changing goes into the fresh index first, so it is searchable within minutes.
In batches, the indexer builds new immutable index files and swaps them onto the shards that own those documents.

deepDives.title: Shard by document or by term
deepDives.question: How do we split an index too big for one machine?

options.name: By document
options.pros: Each shard is a complete small search engine. Adding documents touches one shard. A dead shard loses a slice of results, not whole words.
options.cons: Every query goes to every shard, so cost per query grows with the shard count.

options.name: By term
options.pros: A query goes only to the shards holding its words.
options.cons: Long posting lists must travel between machines to be intersected. Common words create hot shards.

deepDives.because: Intersecting lists locally avoids shipping huge lists over the network. The price is fan-out, which we control with replicas, caches, deadlines and a cap on how much each shard returns.

deepDives.title: Cheap first, costly second
deepDives.question: How do we use a rich ranking model without scoring millions of matches?

options.name: One scoring function everywhere
options.pros: Simple. Every document is scored the same way.
options.cons: Either the model is too weak to be good, or too slow to run on every match.

options.name: Pre-rank by a static quality score
options.pros: Sort posting lists by page quality so a shard can stop early.
options.cons: Quality ignores the query. A good page for this query can be missed.

options.name: Cheap score, then re-rank the top
options.pros: A fast score on every candidate, then the slow model on a few hundred. Models can change independently.
options.cons: If the cheap stage drops a good page, the expensive stage never sees it.

deepDives.because: Order lists by a static quality score so shards can stop early, score cheaply, and re-rank only the top K. Measure recall of the cheap stage, because it caps the final quality.

deepDives.title: Tail latency across the fan-out
deepDives.question: A query waits for the slowest shard. How do we keep it fast when there are hundreds?

options.name: Wait for every shard
options.cons: If each shard is slow 1% of the time, most queries hit at least one slow shard.

options.name: Hard deadline, return what arrived
options.pros: Bounded latency. A missing slice only lowers recall a little.
options.cons: Results vary between runs, and a persistently slow shard hides documents.

options.name: Hedged requests to replicas
options.pros: After a short wait, send the same request to a second replica and take the first reply. Cuts the tail cheaply.
options.cons: Adds some extra load, and needs a replica copy of every shard.

deepDives.because: Send the hedge after, say, the 95th percentile latency, so only a few percent of requests are doubled. Cancel the loser. Keep the deadline as the final safety net.

deepDives.title: Fresh and big index together
deepDives.question: How do new pages become searchable fast without rebuilding a giant index?

options.name: Rebuild everything often
options.cons: Hours to build. Pages are stale in between.

options.name: Update the big index in place
options.cons: Writes fight reads, and compact immutable files are lost.

options.name: Two tiers merged at query time
options.pros: A small index absorbs new pages in minutes. The big one stays immutable and fast.
options.cons: Every query reads both. Fresh results need their own scoring care. Needs a periodic merge.

deepDives.because: Immutable files are what make the big index fast and cacheable. A small mutable tier handles change, and a background job folds it into the big one.

failures.what: One shard is slow or down
failures.impact: The query waits on it, or results from its documents go missing.
failures.fix: Replicas per shard, a deadline, hedged requests, and a degraded answer from the shards that replied.

failures.what: A burst of one hot query
failures.impact: Millions ask the same thing at once, such as a breaking event, and the fan-out multiplies it.
failures.fix: Cache results for a few seconds, and coalesce identical in-flight queries into a single fan-out.

failures.what: A bad index build goes live
failures.impact: Results get worse or empty for the documents in a bad shard.
failures.fix: Build into new files and check them against sample queries first. Swap gradually, and keep the old files to roll back.

failures.impact: Every query waits on the expensive stage.
failures.fix: Give it a time limit. If it runs out, fall back to the cheap ordering. Cap how many candidates go to it.

failures.impact: The small tier gets slow and loses its speed advantage.
failures.fix: Fold it into the big index on a schedule and expire old entries. Alert when its size passes a limit.

scaling.limit: Fan-out cost grows with the number of shards
scaling.lever: Bigger shards, replicas for the query rate, and tiers so most queries touch only a smaller index of the best pages.
Serve from regional clusters, each with replicas of the index, and send each query to the nearest one.
Compress posting lists with delta encoding, keep a small tier of important pages, and drop low-value pages.

recap.key: Invert the web into posting lists, split the index by document, scatter each query to all shards and merge, then spend the costly ranking only on the top few hundred.
recap.numbers: 50B documents at 200M per shard is 250 shards. 100K queries per second means 25M shard requests per second, in a 200 ms budget.
moves: Inverted index: term to sorted posting list of documents
Shard by document, scatter-gather through an aggregator
Cheap first-pass score, then re-rank only the top K
Cache hot queries, hedge slow shards, and add a fresh tier
